title: Hypergeometric Functions: An Evolutionary Algorithm for Optimization
abstract: Hypergeometric Functions (HFs) have emerged as a powerful tool in mathematical modeling and analysis, particularly in the context of statistical physics and data analysis. This paper explores the application of evolutionary algorithms (EAs) to optimize high-dimensional data distributions, offering a novel approach to enhancing the performance of machine learning models. The core claim is that a specifically designed hybrid EAs can efficiently search for optimal HFs, leading to improved data distribution and enhanced machine learning performance. The paper details the design of the evolutionary algorithm, its mechanism, and its potential impact on machine learning, emphasizing its efficiency and adaptability.

title: 基于动态自适应的图神经网络的节点优化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel node optimization strategy based on dynamic self-adaptive neural networks (DANNs). Traditional node optimization methods often rely on manual design, limiting their adaptability to changing data. We propose a DANN-based approach that dynamically adjusts the connections between nodes during training, leading to improved model performance. The core mechanism involves a self-adaptive adjustment algorithm that continuously monitors and adjusts the network's connections based on the training data's characteristics. This allows the network to learn more effectively and generalize better to unseen data. The proposed method offers a flexible and robust solution for optimizing node connectivity in neural networks.

title: Topological Gradient Descent for Neural Network Training
abstract: This paper introduces Topological Gradient Descent (TGD), a novel optimization algorithm that utilizes topological properties to guide the training of neural networks. Traditional gradient descent methods often struggle with convergence and stability due to local optima and sensitivity to initial conditions. TGD leverages a "Topological Gradient" – a measure of network topology – to steer the optimization process, resulting in improved convergence and increased stability. We present a framework for calculating and incorporating the Topological Gradient into the gradient descent process, demonstrating its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and experimental validation. The core mechanism involves constructing a graph representation of the network and employing a dynamic topological gradient update.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel data integration framework leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement to achieve significantly enhanced data processing efficiency and improved data quality. title: Topological Quantum Adaptive Optimization (TDAO)
abstract: This paper introduces TDAO, a novel quantum optimization algorithm designed to address the limitations of traditional optimization methods by dynamically adjusting the quantum potential field during the optimization process. The core mechanism of TDAO involves a dynamic shift in the quantum potential based on the system's inherent dynamics, enabling automated parameter adjustments that lead to improved efficiency. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental validation demonstrating the effectiveness of TDAO in solving complex optimization problems. The paper explores the advantages of this approach over existing quantum algorithms and highlights its potential impact across diverse fields.

title: Neural Network Topology-Driven Dynamic Program Generation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neuro-inspired programming by leveraging the dynamic topology of neural networks. Traditional neural network modeling often relies on static, fixed architectures, limiting adaptability and learning capabilities. Our method addresses this limitation by employing a system that extracts topological information – including connection strengths, patterns, and local clusters – from simulated neural network activity. This extracted topology is then utilized by generative algorithms, specifically Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) or Genetic Algorithms, to automatically generate dynamic rules controlling neural network behavior. These rules are designed to adapt to new inputs or environmental changes and are continuously optimized through feedback mechanisms. The core innovation lies in treating the neural network as a dynamic system governed by its topology, enabling the creation of programs with enhanced adaptability and learning. The system's ability to dynamically modify neural network behavior offers a significant advancement in neuro-inspired programming and control.

title: Neural Simulation via a Probabilistic Information Theory Framework
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for simulating neural networks based on probabilistic information theory. The core idea is to treat neural simulations as processes of probabilistic information handling, leveraging concepts like entropy and mutual information to model synaptic transmission and learning mechanisms. Traditional neural models often rely on discrete mathematical descriptions, which can be overly simplified and lack the nuanced probabilistic behavior observed in biological systems. This work introduces a mechanism for defining the probability distribution governing synaptic transmission and explicitly linking it to learning rules. The resulting model provides a more biologically plausible representation of neural computation, offering potential advantages for understanding and modeling complex neural phenomena. The framework addresses the limitations of existing approaches by incorporating information theory, providing a probabilistic foundation for neural simulation.

title: Quantum Entanglement Reservoir Computing for Complex System Modeling
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to complex system modeling utilizing quantum entanglement as a dynamically configurable reservoir. Traditional recurrent neural networks often struggle with high-dimensional data and capturing complex temporal dependencies. We propose a Quantum Entanglement Reservoir Computing (QERC) framework where system inputs are directly mapped to entangled qubit states. The reservoir's evolution is governed by weak, time-dependent interactions, enabling non-linear mapping and the emergence of rich temporal correlations. The correlated qubit output, upon measurement, directly reflects the system state. This method offers a potentially significant advantage over conventional approaches by exploiting the inherent redundancy and correlations within quantum entanglement, providing a more robust and efficient representation of complex dynamics. The core claim of this work is the utilization of quantum entanglement as a dynamically configurable reservoir to represent complex, high-dimensional system dynamics, bypassing the limitations of traditional recurrent neural networks. The core mechanism involves mapping system inputs directly to entangled qubit states, with reservoir evolution driven by weak, time-dependent interactions, facilitating non-linear mapping and emergent temporal correlations. Measurement of correlated qubit output directly reflects the system state. ---

title: Quantum State Tomography for Hardware Verification of Quantum Computers
abstract: Quantum state tomography (QST) is a fundamental technique for characterizing quantum states, traditionally employed in research laboratories with highly controlled environments. However, the burgeoning field of quantum computing faces the significant challenge of deploying and verifying quantum hardware in the presence of noise and decoherence, characteristics inherent in current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. This paper proposes an adapted QST algorithm designed to overcome these limitations. The core idea is to systematically reconstruct the density matrix of a qubit or a small quantum system using a series of carefully designed measurements. We address the impact of noise by incorporating error mitigation strategies within the reconstruction process. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through theoretical analysis and conceptual implementation, highlighting its potential to provide a practical and efficient method for hardware verification of NISQ computers. This work establishes a novel approach for characterizing and debugging NISQ hardware, a critical step toward realizing the full potential of quantum computation.

title: Meta-Learning for Domain Adaptation
abstract: Domain adaptation is a crucial technique in machine learning for addressing the problem of performance degradation when applying models trained on one domain (source) to a different domain (target). Traditional domain adaptation methods often rely on large amounts of labeled target data, which is frequently unavailable or expensive to acquire. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging meta-learning to facilitate rapid domain adaptation. The core idea is to pre-train a model on multiple source domains to acquire generalized knowledge, and then utilize meta-learning algorithms to efficiently adjust the model parameters based on limited target domain data. This approach significantly reduces the reliance on target domain labels and demonstrates improved adaptation performance compared to conventional domain adaptation methods. The key contributions of this work include the integration of meta-learning with domain adaptation and the demonstration of its effectiveness in scenarios with limited target domain data.

title: Probability Logic Reasoning and Uncertainty Computation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel computational model designed to address the challenges of probability logic reasoning and uncertainty computation. Traditional logical systems struggle to effectively incorporate probabilistic information, leading to limitations in solving complex problems where uncertainty plays a significant role. Our approach combines elements from probability logic, fuzzy logic, and Bayesian networks to create a hybrid system capable of handling both logical deduction and probabilistic inference. The core mechanism involves representing knowledge as a network of interconnected nodes, each associated with a probability distribution and a logical value. This allows for the propagation of both logical consequences and probabilistic updates throughout the network. We demonstrate the model's ability to solve problems requiring reasoning under uncertainty, offering a more robust and flexible solution compared to conventional approaches. The key contribution lies in the synergistic integration of these logical paradigms, providing a framework for intelligent systems to navigate situations characterized by incomplete and conflicting information. The model is presented with a focus on its theoretical foundations and conceptual design, providing a basis for future development and implementation. ---

title: 基于量子退火算法的复杂优化问题求解
abstract: This paper investigates the application of the Quantum Annealing (QA) algorithm to solve complex optimization problems. The core claim is that simulating a complex optimization problem's local search process through the QA's annealing process can effectively locate global optimal solutions. The mechanism involves mapping the solution space of an optimization problem onto the annealing path of QA, controlling the annealing rate and path to guide the solution towards the optimal point. This research leverages QA's inherent ability to mimic physical annealing, aiming to enhance optimization efficiency and accuracy. We present a framework for formulating and applying QA to various complex problems, highlighting its potential advantages over traditional optimization methods. This work contributes to the growing field of quantum computing by demonstrating a practical approach to tackling challenging optimization tasks. The results suggest that QA can be a viable alternative for achieving superior performance in specific optimization scenarios.

title: Contextualized Reinforcement Learning with Memory Networks
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in various domains, but its application to complex, long-horizon tasks remains a significant challenge. Traditional RL algorithms often struggle with incomplete or sparse reward signals, leading to slow learning and difficulty in capturing long-term dependencies. This paper proposes a novel approach to contextualized reinforcement learning by integrating Memory Networks (MNs) into the RL agent. The core idea is to enable the agent to store and retrieve relevant experiences from its past, effectively augmenting its experience replay buffer and facilitating the learning of complex, temporally extended tasks. The MN component acts as an external memory, storing state-action-reward tuples alongside contextual information. When the agent encounters a new state, the MN is queried to retrieve relevant past experiences, which are then used to guide the current action selection. We hypothesize that this contextualization of experience will dramatically improve the agent's ability to learn long-horizon tasks by providing a richer representation of the environment and enabling more efficient exploration. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and a conceptual design, outlining the key components and interactions within the system. Future work will focus on implementing and evaluating this architecture in simulated environments.

title: Discovering Translation-Worthy Languages with E-Values
abstract: Choosing when to translate multilingual documents is a central routing problem in text classification: translation can improve predictions for some languages while degrading others or adding unnecessary computation. Uniform translation and heuristic language tiers do not provide statistically controlled route selection. We introduce a language-level router based on paired e-processes that continuously compares direct and translation-assisted classification before freezing a routing policy. A familywise-controlled threshold of 280 bounds the probability of any false route across 14 eligible languages per dataset by 0.05. On SIB-200 and MASSIVE, the router selects translation for 4 of 15 languages and 14 of 15 locales, improving held-out accuracy over direct classification by 8.14 and 16.70 percentage points, respectively. All 28 decisions remain stable across 50 outcome-independent orderings and relative to the per-group threshold. Our results demonstrate that paired e-processes enable statistically controlled, anytime-valid, and auditable multilingual classification routing.

title: Title: Epistemic Morphing (EM)
abstract: This paper introduces Epistemic Morphing (EM), a computational framework for evolving mathematical structures – specifically, geometric predicates – through iterative self-reference. EM provides a novel mechanism for creating self-replicating proofs and geometric models, enabling continuous mathematical evolution. The core of the system involves refining a mathematical predicate by applying it to its own output, driving the dynamic system to produce new proofs and geometric models. This approach offers a potential pathway for discovering new mathematical theorems and algorithms by systematically exploring variations and combinations of existing structures. The paper details the EM process, provides an illustrative example, and discusses potential applications and future research directions.

title: Quantum Machine Learning Adaptive Optimizer
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) presents a paradigm shift in computational paradigms, offering the potential for breakthroughs in various fields, including machine learning. This paper explores the application of Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) to a novel adaptive optimization framework, termed "Quantum Adaptive Optimizer" (QAO). We detail the fundamental principles of QAO, emphasizing its reliance on quantum error correction and quantum entanglement to enhance the optimization process. The core mechanism centers around leveraging QNNs' inherent ability to represent and manipulate complex data through quantum algorithms, allowing for automatic adaptation to evolving problem landscapes. This research investigates the potential of QAO to overcome limitations of classical optimization techniques, particularly in scenarios demanding high precision and resilience in dynamic environments. The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges and future directions of this innovative approach.

title: Self-Adaptive Quantum Error Correction Protocol for Quantum Entanglement
abstract: Quantum computing promises revolutionary advancements across diverse fields, but its inherent fragility – the susceptibility to decoherence and errors – presents significant challenges. Quantum error correction is crucial for achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation, but traditional methods often struggle with the complex dynamics of quantum systems and the inevitable degradation of entanglement. This paper proposes a novel self-adaptive quantum error correction protocol, designed to mitigate the effects of entanglement loss through dynamic adjustment of error correction strength and strategic entanglement management. We present a framework incorporating a dynamically adaptive error correction scheme, incorporating a tailored entanglement management strategy, and exploring its potential to significantly enhance the reliability of quantum computations. The proposed protocol leverages feedback mechanisms to optimize the correction process, minimizing the impact of decoherence and increasing the fidelity of quantum states. This work contributes to the development of robust quantum error correction strategies, paving the way for more reliable and scalable quantum technologies.

title: Quantum Simulation of Non-Linear Geometry Correction
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum simulation to address limitations in classical geometric modeling, particularly concerning error correction and improved accuracy. We propose a novel geometric correction algorithm leveraging quantum entanglement and superposition to minimize discrepancies inherent in geometric representations. The core mechanism involves a quantum-enhanced adjustment of geometric parameters within the simulation, guided by the principles of quantum geometry. The goal is to develop a method that surpasses the capabilities of traditional approaches, offering a pathway towards more robust and accurate geometric simulations. The paper details the underlying theoretical framework, the proposed algorithm's mechanics, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the algorithm's efficacy in correcting geometric distortions.

title: Title: Dynamic Constraint-Based Graph Embedding for Adaptive Machine Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic constraint-based graph embedding method designed to facilitate adaptive machine learning. Traditional graph embedding techniques often rely on pre-defined structural constraints, limiting the model's flexibility and hindering the ability to automatically generate hierarchical structures. Our approach leverages reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust graph structure during training, optimizing for both accuracy and efficiency. We propose a framework that iteratively constructs graphs, leveraging node features and relationships to guide the learning process. The core of our method is a reinforcement learning agent that evaluates graph structures and adjusts parameters to improve performance. This allows for the creation of adaptive graphs that can better represent the data and improve the performance of subsequent machine learning tasks. The dynamic nature of the graph structure is crucial for handling complex datasets and optimizing for specific problem requirements. The paper details the architecture, training procedure, and evaluation results demonstrating the effectiveness of this dynamic constraint-based approach.

title: Title: Dynamic Constraint-Based Evolutionary Algorithm for Machine Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel evolutionary algorithm, termed the Dynamic Constraint-Based Evolutionary Algorithm (DCBAE), designed to accelerate the learning of machine learning models and improve model performance through adaptive constraint management. Traditional evolutionary algorithms often rely on fixed constraints, limiting the potential for rapid optimization. The DCBAE dynamically adjusts constraints during the learning process, responding to model progress and optimizing for both accuracy and efficiency. This approach addresses the limitations of static constraint systems, offering a more responsive and effective method for training complex models. We present a detailed theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the benefits of the DCBAE in various machine learning tasks.

title: Quantum Entanglement: A Probability Tensor Model
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a significant challenge to classical computational approaches. This paper explores the development of a probabilistic tensor model to represent and simulate the complexities of quantum information processing, aiming to enhance the efficiency of quantum computation. We propose a novel approach utilizing tensor operations to model entanglement measurements, offering a potential pathway to more streamlined and efficient quantum algorithms. The core claim is that the established probabilistic tensor model, when properly implemented, can provide a robust and scalable framework for analyzing and manipulating entanglement, ultimately contributing to increased computational capabilities within the quantum realm.

title: 基于异质性信息的自适应算法设计
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm for optimization and search based on the incorporation of inherent heterogeneity within the input data. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameter settings, failing to adequately address the dynamic nature of complex problems. This work introduces a dynamic adjustment mechanism that leverages the distribution of data points to dynamically adjust algorithm parameters and strategies, resulting in improved search efficiency, enhanced robustness, and the ability to effectively navigate challenging scenarios. The core of this algorithm hinges on identifying and utilizing the inherent heterogeneity present within the input data, adapting the optimization process in real-time to maintain optimal performance. We detail the algorithm's architecture, the rationale behind its key components, and provide a comprehensive analysis of its performance through illustrative examples. The resulting algorithm demonstrates superior results compared to conventional approaches, particularly in situations characterized by significant data variability and complex constraints.

title: Self-Referential Quantum Algorithms for Recursive Computation
abstract: This paper explores the concept of self-referential quantum algorithms, proposing a novel framework for recursive computation using quantum mechanics. The core idea is to design algorithms where the output of a computation is fed back as input, allowing for iterative refinement and the potential to tackle problems that are computationally intractable for classical computers. We detail a theoretical mechanism involving feedback loops, emphasizing the creation of self-referential computations. The algorithm's efficiency hinges on leveraging quantum superposition and interference to explore multiple computational paths simultaneously. This approach offers a potential paradigm shift in quantum algorithm design, moving beyond sequential execution to embrace recursive processes. The theoretical framework presented here lays the groundwork for future research into self-referential quantum computation and its applications across diverse scientific and engineering domains. We investigate the mathematical underpinnings of this approach, focusing on the manipulation of quantum states and the design of iterative feedback mechanisms. The core of the algorithm is rooted in the principle of unitary transformations applied repeatedly, culminating in a state representing the solution. The key challenge lies in managing the complexity of these iterative processes and ensuring convergence to a desired outcome. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions and highlighting the significant implications of self-referential quantum algorithms for the advancement of computational science.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Programming via Dynamic Bayesian Circuit Synthesis
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for neuro-symbolic programming, termed Dynamic Bayesian Circuit Synthesis. The core idea is that complex programming tasks can be effectively represented and executed by dynamically constructing Bayesian circuits. These circuits integrate the strengths of neural networks – pattern recognition and learning – with symbolic reasoning – precise rule application and logical deduction. We propose an algorithm that translates a given programming problem into a Bayesian circuit, where nodes correspond to neural network components and edges represent symbolic rules and logical operators. This dynamic synthesis allows for adaptable solutions, particularly in scenarios where the underlying problem structure is evolving or partially unknown. The approach offers a potentially more robust and interpretable method for bridging the gap between neural networks and symbolic AI, moving beyond static architectures and enabling systems that can reason and learn in a truly integrated manner. The key innovation lies in the dynamic, data-driven nature of the circuit construction, allowing the system to adapt to the specific characteristics of the programming task.

title: Dynamic Graph Embedding with Meta-Learning for Few-Shot Node Representation Learning
abstract: Graph representation learning aims to learn meaningful embeddings for nodes in a graph, which can then be utilized in downstream tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. However, many existing graph embedding methods rely on massive amounts of training data, rendering them impractical for scenarios where only a small number of labeled nodes or graphs are available – a situation often encountered in few-shot learning scenarios. This paper introduces a novel approach to dynamic graph embedding by integrating meta-learning. Our method utilizes meta-learning to train a graph embedding model that can quickly adapt to new graph structures with limited training data. The core idea is to leverage the knowledge acquired from embedding previously seen graphs to accelerate the learning process on new graphs. We formulate the problem as a meta-learning task where the embedding model learns a good initialization and update strategy. The model learns to quickly adapt its parameters based on a small number of training samples from the target graph. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in learning high-quality node representations for few-shot graph learning. The key contributions of this work are the introduction of meta-learning into graph embedding and the development of a dynamic embedding strategy that adapts effectively to new graphs with limited data.

title: Towards Explainable AI Decision Agents
abstract: This paper presents a framework for constructing Explainable AI (XAI) decision agents designed to provide transparent and understandable reasoning behind their decisions. The core approach leverages rule-based or case-based reasoning techniques to decompose complex decision-making processes into discrete, interpretable steps and their corresponding justifications. Unlike traditional AI systems which often operate as black boxes, this framework prioritizes explainability alongside predictive accuracy. We detail the architecture of the agent, the rationale behind employing rule and case-based methods, and discuss potential challenges and future research directions. The key objective is to build decision agents that not only make accurate predictions but also offer clear explanations of *why* those predictions were made, fostering trust and facilitating human-AI collaboration. ---

title: Parallel Algorithm Optimization Based on Bio-Inspired Genetic Algorithm
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to optimizing parallel algorithms by leveraging the principles of the genetic algorithm (GA). The core idea is to mimic the evolutionary processes found in nature, specifically variation, crossover, and selection, to refine the parameters within a parallel algorithm. The goal is to enhance the algorithm's performance and efficiency. This work presents a framework for applying GA operators to parallel algorithm tuning, focusing on improving aspects such as execution time, resource utilization, and overall solution quality. The methodology is described and discussed, emphasizing the potential benefits of a bio-inspired optimization technique for complex parallel computational problems. The theoretical foundation and practical implications of this approach are presented, demonstrating the feasibility and effectiveness of using a GA to drive parallel algorithm improvements.

title: Neural Network Topology-Driven Program Synthesis
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to neural network design termed "Topology-Driven Program Synthesis," which leverages large-scale neuronal connectomes to generate networks with desired functionalities. The core idea is to move beyond manual design, relying instead on deep learning models to learn from the structural and connection patterns inherent in biological neural networks. Specifically, we employ techniques such as variational autoencoders (VAE) and generative adversarial networks (GAN) to extract representations from connectome data and subsequently construct corresponding neural network architectures and weights tailored to a specified objective. This approach offers the potential for creating networks with enhanced biological realism and improved performance compared to traditional program synthesis methods that often rely on predefined architectures or manual rules. The presented methodology aims to bridge the gap between biological plausibility and computational efficiency in neural network design.

title: Contextualized Semantic Graph Embeddings with Latent Dialect Modeling
abstract: Graph embeddings have become a cornerstone of modern graph analysis, providing dense vector representations of nodes and edges for downstream tasks. However, existing approaches often struggle to capture the inherent semantic variations that arise when considering a graph's context or 'dialect'. This work introduces a novel framework for contextualized graph embeddings, leveraging latent dialect modeling to learn node representations conditioned on both the surrounding graph structure and node attributes. Our approach constructs a latent dialect model that learns a distributed representation of graph semantics, effectively capturing context-specific nuances. The core mechanism involves learning a probabilistic model that predicts node features given the surrounding graph context, resulting in embeddings that are sensitive to the specific environment in which a node resides. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and illustrate its potential with a conceptual example. The goal is to create more accurate and robust graph embeddings by explicitly incorporating contextual information.

title: Title: Adaptive Information Encoding via Neural Resonance Networks
abstract: This paper introduces an innovative approach to information encoding within neural networks, termed Adaptive Information Encoding (AIE). AIE leverages a novel layer that dynamically calculates a 'resonance score' for each connection and activation, allowing for self-correction and enhanced generalization. The core mechanism centers around adjusting weights and connections to maximize this resonance, creating a feedback loop that iteratively improves the network's representation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AIE through extensive experiments on a range of benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in performance and robustness compared to traditional methods. The research explores how this adaptive approach mitigates overfitting and facilitates the learning of complex, nuanced patterns within data.

title: Quantum State Collapse as a Computational Step
abstract: This paper explores the intriguing possibility of utilizing quantum state collapse as a fundamental computational step. We propose a novel "state-collapse algorithm" designed to precisely control the transition of quantum states, offering a potential pathway to simulating complex physical systems with unprecedented accuracy. The core mechanism centers on manipulating quantum states through carefully orchestrated interventions, mirroring the collapse of quantum systems themselves. We outline the algorithm's structure, demonstrate its preliminary results through simplified examples, and discuss the implications for future computational advancements. This work investigates whether this approach could represent a paradigm shift in computational capabilities, moving beyond the inherent limitations of classical methods.

title: Systematic review and comparative synthesis of cross lingual question answering systems for low resource Indic languages
abstract: Recent advancements in Question Answering (QA) methods on resource-rich languages have significantly improved answer accuracy and contextual understanding performance. However, extending these capabilities to low-resource Indic languages remains a persistent challenge. This study carries out a systematic review of 137 shortlisted research articles, and a detailed comparative synthesis of 78 core articles is further conducted by considering dataset diversity, modelling paradigms, alignment strategies, and evaluation frameworks across extractive, generative, and conversational QA systems. To improve analytical rigour and follow a systematic review process, four Research Questions (RQs) are defined to verify dataset suitability, cross-lingual alignment strategies, adaptation mechanisms, and evaluation outcomes. The review additionally explores recent advancements and methods used in building QA systems with a primary focus on learning multilingual datasets, pre-trained language models, cross-lingual transfer methods, and evaluation metrics specifically tailored for Indic languages. Even though language-specific models utilize fine-grained linguistic features, a comparative analysis shows that the multilingual models’ broader representation and transfer capabilities help them perform better than language-specific frameworks. In general, the review findings indicate that the performance variations are more context-specific rather than consistent across different datasets, task formulations, and alignment strategies. In contrast to existing QA surveys, the proposed review offers an Indic-centred synthesis that explicitly relates to dataset design, alignment paradigms, and evaluation practices to other structural linguistic variables such as morphology richness, script diversity, and typological divergence. The review findings reveal that the performance of a cross-lingual QA system is structurally influenced by the interaction between linguistic typology, model design, and not exclusively by model scale or architecture.

title: NOVA: Normal-Side Modeling for Training-Free Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection
abstract: Training-free zero-shot video anomaly detection (ZS-VAD) leverages vision-language models (VLMs) to localize anomaly instances from a predefined anomaly vocabulary, without providing any video. Existing CLIP-based methods often emphasize anomaly-side semantics, while the competing normality side remains less carefully formulated. We identify two key limitations in existing solutions: (i) blurred decision boundary: normal prompts may contain ambiguous verbs, such as running, that are semantically close to anomalies, reducing normal and abnormal separation in the VLM embedding space; and (ii) modality gap: poor alignment between features of textual normal anchors and visual frames. We propose NOVA, a training-free ZS-VAD framework that strengthens the normal side at both linguistic and visual levels. NOVA introduces Normality-Aware Prompt Construction (NA), which excludes anomaly-adjacent verbs and biases normal descriptions toward static, low-motion scenes. To overcome the text-vision modality gap, NOVA constructs a Visual Normality Anchor (VNA), which creates a weighted visual normal anchor from the initial frames of each test video, providing a video-specific normal reference without task-specific training or annotations. NOVA achieves 89.86 percent AUC on UCF-Crime and 95.07 percent AUC and 84.82 percent AP on XD-Violence, reaching state-of-the-art performance among comparable training-free zero-shot methods.

title: Neural-Symbolic Integration Models: Complexity Assessment and Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the complexity of Neural-Symbolic Integration (NSI) models, a burgeoning field aiming to combine the strengths of neural networks and symbolic reasoning. We propose a novel framework for automated complexity assessment, leveraging a multi-faceted evaluation approach centered on knowledge coverage and reasoning capability. The framework incorporates a dynamic weighting system to prioritize key metrics, providing actionable optimization suggestions. The core mechanism involves integrating neural network representations with symbolic rule-based systems, systematically assessing the model's ability to learn and apply this hybrid knowledge. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of quantitative experiments, showcasing improved performance and enhanced interpretability compared to existing methods. The study highlights the potential of this framework for advancing the design and understanding of complex NSI models.

title: Quantum Topology for Scalable Quantum Computation
abstract: Quantum computation, leveraging the unique properties of quantum mechanics, holds immense potential for scientific discovery and technological advancement. However, scaling quantum systems to larger numbers poses significant challenges, primarily due to the difficulty in controlling and manipulating complex quantum states. This paper proposes a novel approach to quantum computation based on self-adaptive topology, offering a pathway towards more efficient and scalable quantum circuits. We introduce a framework that dynamically adjusts the topology of a quantum network to optimize performance based on the desired quantum algorithm. The core mechanism focuses on intelligently restructuring the network's connections to minimize errors and maximize fidelity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a simplified model and preliminary results on a small-scale quantum circuit simulator. The potential implications of this research lie in significantly enhancing the speed and robustness of quantum computations, paving the way for more practical quantum algorithms.

title: 基于自适应的自适应机器学习框架
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive machine learning framework that dynamically adjusts model parameters and learning strategies based on the data distribution and model predictions. Traditional machine learning models often struggle with complex datasets, necessitating a method for adaptive learning. This work proposes a framework that iteratively refines model parameters through a process of self-tuning, enhancing model generalization and performance. The core mechanism involves a dynamic parameter adjustment algorithm driven by a feedback loop that continuously evaluates model performance against the data, guiding parameter updates towards optimal solution. This approach offers a significant advancement over static model optimization techniques, promising improved accuracy and robustness in various machine learning applications.

title: Probability Geometric Adaptive Optimization
abstract: Probability geometric adaptive optimization presents a novel approach to optimization by leveraging the power of probability distributions to model system states and dynamically adjust optimization objectives. This research explores the application of probabilistic frameworks within an adaptive optimization framework, aiming to surpass traditional methods by incorporating self-adaptation and robust solution exploration. We propose a new algorithm that utilizes a probability distribution as a core component, allowing the system to adapt its behavior based on the inherent uncertainty within the problem. The core mechanism involves a dynamic parameter adjustment process guided by the probability distribution, ensuring a pathway toward global optimality. The work demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations and analysis, highlighting its potential to address challenges inherent in traditional optimization techniques.

title: Topological Information Theory: A Novel Approach to Data Compression and Cryptography
abstract: This paper introduces Topological Information Theory (TIT) as a novel framework for data compression and cryptography. We propose a new method centered on the integration of topological properties with information theory, specifically focusing on self-similarity and non-self-similarity. The core concept is the "拓扑数据结构" (Topological Data Structure), which dynamically adapts to the underlying data structure, enabling efficient compression and enhanced security. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through the implementation of a data compression algorithm and a cryptographic scheme based on topological transformations. The research explores the potential of leveraging the inherent structure of topological data to achieve superior compression ratios and robust security guarantees.

title: Core Claim: Design a dynamic topology-based geometric group capable of self-adaptive adjustment of its sub-structure, thereby enabling more efficient complex computations, such as quantum computing or cryptography.
abstract: The study of geometric groups and their applications, particularly in areas like quantum computing and cryptography, presents a significant challenge in optimizing complex computations. Traditional approaches often involve designing and implementing specific sub-structures, which can limit the overall efficiency of these computations. This paper proposes a novel approach to geometric group optimization based on dynamic topology, utilizing a topological generator module to adaptively adjust the group's sub-structure during computation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through the implementation of a simplified, yet representative, example of a geometric group, showcasing its ability to achieve improved computational efficiency compared to traditional methods. The core mechanism involves generating new sub-structures based on the current state and target, and maintaining a topology tree to represent these relationships. This allows for a more flexible and adaptive optimization process, opening up new possibilities for enhancing the performance of complex computations.

title: 基于自适应的量子机器学习的特征选择算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to feature selection using a quantum machine learning algorithm, specifically designed for dynamic feature selection based on data characteristics. Traditional feature selection methods often rely on static selection strategies, failing to fully exploit the intricacies of the data. This research leverages the unique capabilities of quantum computing to dynamically adjust feature selection strategies, resulting in improved model performance and enhanced predictive accuracy. We introduce a quantum-enhanced feature selection framework that adapts to the data's evolution, offering a significant advantage over conventional techniques. The core mechanism centers around quantum optimization and adaptive feature weighting, allowing for a more comprehensive and efficient exploration of the feature space. We detail the algorithm's design, demonstrate its efficacy through illustrative examples, and analyze its potential impact on machine learning models. The paper concludes with a discussion of future directions and potential applications.

title: Title: Neuro-Lattice Geometry: Mapping Neural Networks to Lattice Structures
abstract: This paper explores the novel concept of Neuro-Lattice Geometry, a framework for representing and analyzing neural networks by mapping their structure to lattice geometries. We propose a dynamic mapping algorithm that converts network connectivity and activation patterns into geometric representations, offering a potential bridge between neural network dynamics and fundamental geometric principles. The core claim is that this mapping allows for a deeper understanding of network representation, potentially revealing insights into learning, generalization, and the underlying structure of complex systems. The paper details the development of this mapping algorithm, outlines its theoretical foundations, and presents preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in visualizing and analyzing neural network representations.

title: Title: Non-Euclidean Data Structures for Machine Learning
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of novel data structures inspired by non-Euclidean geometry to enhance machine learning algorithms, particularly in the context of high-dimensional spaces. Traditional data structures often struggle with the inherent complexities of data distribution and require significant computational resources. We propose a new data structure, tentatively named the "Hypercube Network," which utilizes hyperplanes and curves to represent data, enabling more efficient exploration and optimization within high-dimensional spaces. The core mechanism centers around the creation of interconnected nodes representing data points, with the ability to traverse and manipulate these nodes through hyperplanes. We explore the potential benefits of this approach, focusing on improved representation, optimization, and the handling of sparse data scenarios commonly encountered in machine learning. This work presents a theoretical framework and preliminary implementation demonstrating the feasibility of this new data structure.

title: Adaptive Hierarchical Symbolic Regression with Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) is a powerful technique for discovering mathematical equations from data. However, its scalability and the inherent challenge of quantifying uncertainty in the resulting models remain significant limitations. This paper presents an adaptive hierarchical symbolic regression framework that addresses these issues. The framework employs a multi-level search strategy, dynamically adjusting the complexity of the search space based on observed data and Bayesian inference. This allows for efficient exploration of the solution space while simultaneously providing robust uncertainty estimates for the discovered symbolic expressions. The core claim is that combining hierarchical search with Bayesian methods offers a significant improvement in both the efficiency and reliability of symbolic regression. The key mechanism involves a dynamically adjusting search tree and Bayesian inference for confidence quantification. The system learns to prioritize exploration of regions with higher predictive accuracy and higher confidence, leading to the discovery of more accurate and reliable equations. This approach provides a novel solution to the longstanding challenges in symbolic regression, paving the way for its broader application in various scientific and engineering domains.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning via Temporal Logic
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to reasoning systems by fusing the strengths of neural networks and symbolic logic. Traditional neural networks often struggle with reasoning about temporal relationships and structured knowledge, while symbolic systems lack the flexibility and adaptability to handle noisy or uncertain perceptual data. We propose a neuro-symbolic architecture that leverages neural networks for perception and symbolic reasoning, specifically using temporal logic, to represent and manipulate temporal relationships. The core innovation lies in formally integrating these two paradigms, allowing the system to reason about events and their evolution over time with greater robustness and interpretability. The system is designed to learn perceptual features from raw data using neural networks, and then translate these features into logical statements within a temporal logic framework for reasoning. This approach addresses the challenges of knowledge representation and inference in dynamic environments. We outline the system's architecture, the temporal logic representation scheme, and discuss key considerations for training and deployment. The system demonstrates the potential for improved reasoning performance compared to purely neural or purely symbolic approaches.

title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Abstract State Representation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) framework designed to enhance the scalability and efficiency of RL agents operating in complex environments. The core innovation lies in the introduction of a "state abstraction layer" employing a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to learn abstract, high-level state representations from raw sensory input. This layer dynamically maps the initial state space into a more manageable and meaningful latent space, which is then leveraged by higher-level RL agents for decision-making. The framework aims to mitigate the curse of dimensionality typically encountered in RL, allowing agents to operate at a more strategic level, significantly reducing the computational burden. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline the key components and algorithms involved. The system is designed to learn a compact representation of the environment, leading to faster learning and improved generalization performance. Further research will explore specific implementation details and evaluate the framework across diverse benchmark environments.

title: Symbolic Regression with Evolutionary Constraint Satisfaction
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to symbolic regression, integrating evolutionary search with constraint satisfaction techniques. The core idea is to automatically discover mathematical equations that best fit given data, while simultaneously respecting predefined domain constraints. The algorithm utilizes a symbolic tree representation for equations and employs an evolutionary algorithm to explore the search space. Crucially, constraint satisfaction algorithms are used to prune unproductive branches of the tree, ensuring that only equations meeting the specified constraints are considered. This hybrid approach aims to produce more accurate and interpretable mathematical models compared to traditional symbolic regression methods. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and a detailed explanation of the underlying mechanisms, without requiring empirical experimental validation. The key contributions lie in the synergistic combination of evolutionary optimization and constraint-driven search, resulting in a robust and efficient symbolic regression engine.

title: Based on Dynamic Topology Embedding for Neural Symbolic Reasoning
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to neural symbolic reasoning by leveraging dynamic topology embedding. Traditional neural symbolic reasoning methods often rely on fixed, pre-defined symbolic representations and inference rules, which can be inflexible and struggle with complex, real-world problems. We propose a framework where the topology of a neural network is allowed to evolve dynamically during the reasoning process. This evolution is guided by a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that learns to adjust the network's connection weights based on the success or failure of inferences. The core claim is that dynamic topology adjustment significantly enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of neural symbolic reasoning. The key mechanism involves a feedback loop where the RL agent optimizes the network's structure to better represent and manipulate the underlying symbolic knowledge. This approach moves beyond static architectures, allowing for a more adaptive and robust reasoning process. We detail the architecture, the RL training procedure, and discuss potential applications and future research directions.

title: Graph-Based Representation of Linguistic Semantics for Natural Language Understanding
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to natural language understanding (NLU) based on graph representation of linguistic semantics. Traditional methods like word embeddings often struggle to capture the intricate relationships between words and concepts, leading to limitations in understanding nuanced meaning. We introduce a system that constructs a graph where nodes represent concepts and relations, and edges represent the semantic connections derived from linguistic analysis and knowledge bases. This graph-based representation allows for a more accurate and flexible modeling of semantic information, addressing the shortcomings of static word embeddings. title: Based on Bio-Inspired Algorithms for Compiler Optimization
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to compiler optimization by leveraging bio-inspired algorithms, specifically a genetic algorithm, to mimic the process of biological evolution. Traditional compiler optimization techniques often rely on hand-crafted heuristics and static analysis, which can be limited in their ability to explore the vast solution space and adapt to diverse code characteristics. This research transforms the compiler optimization problem into an optimization problem suitable for evolutionary algorithms. The algorithm iteratively generates candidate optimization solutions (chromosomes) through mutation and crossover operations, evaluating their effectiveness based on metrics like code size, execution speed, and instruction count. The fittest solutions are then selected for reproduction, leading to a population that gradually evolves towards optimal solutions. The core claim is that this approach, by simulating biological evolution, enables the discovery of more intelligent and effective optimization strategies compared to traditional methods. This paper details the framework, the implementation, and a preliminary evaluation of the proposed system, highlighting its potential benefits and future research directions.

title: Constrained Bayesian Optimization for Hierarchical Federated Learning in IoT Networks for Plant Disease Classification
abstract: The deployment of Hierarchical Federated Learning (HFL) in resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) environments requires careful configuration to balance predictive performance with energy consumption and execution time. This challenge is particularly relevant to smart agriculture, where distributed IoT devices can support automated plant disease classification while operating under limited computational and communication resources. This paper presents a constrained Bayesian Optimization framework for the efficient configuration of HFL deployments. The proposed approach jointly explores the deep learning backbone architecture, aggregation strategy, and number of communication rounds, while the federation size is determined according to the spatial coverage requirements of the agricultural deployment. A weighted objective function captures user-defined trade-offs among energy consumption, execution time, and predictive performance, while explicit constraints ensure compliance with deployment-specific resource and accuracy requirements. The framework is evaluated on an IoT-based plant disease classification task considering multiple deep learning architectures, federated aggregation strategies, and communication-round settings. Experimental results across 30 independent optimization runs show that the proposed approach explores only 11.11% of the search space, while consistently identifying solutions within 1% of the exhaustive-search optimum, with a mean optimality gap of only 0.056%.

title: Non-Linear Matrix Decomposition Adaptive Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel non-linear matrix decomposition-based adaptive optimization algorithm designed to address the challenges of large-scale optimization. Traditional approaches often rely on fixed parameter settings, limiting efficiency when data characteristics and function complexities vary. Our algorithm dynamically adjusts the decomposition strategy based on learned data features and function properties, achieving superior optimization performance through automated parameter tuning. We present a comprehensive theoretical analysis and practical implementation demonstrating the algorithm's effectiveness on diverse benchmark datasets. The core mechanism utilizes a dynamic matrix decomposition framework, incorporating a learning component to adapt to the data. This adaptability significantly enhances optimization efficiency compared to static methods. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's limitations and potential future directions.

title: Self-Adaptive Topological Structures for Quantum Computing: A Dynamic Mapping Approach
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic mapping technique for quantum computing based on self-adaptive topological structures. The core idea is to dynamically adjust the quantum system's topology during computation, allowing for enhanced reliability and performance. We explore a method that iteratively modifies the quantum system's topology based on the evolution of the quantum state, leading to improved outcomes in complex calculations. The proposed approach addresses limitations of existing mapping techniques by offering a highly adaptable and robust framework. The paper details the theoretical foundations, the implementation of the dynamic mapping process, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the technique's effectiveness in a specific quantum algorithm. The focus is on showcasing the potential of this method to significantly improve the robustness of quantum computations.

title: Geometric Complexity Analysis in Quantum Algorithms
abstract: Quantum algorithms, renowned for their potential to surpass classical algorithms in certain tasks, are notoriously sensitive to their underlying structure. Geometric complexity, a measure of the algorithm's state space and its associated computational burden, plays a crucial role in determining its efficiency. This paper investigates a novel method for quantifying geometric complexity, offering a tool for automated algorithm design. We propose a new measure based on the topological structure of the quantum state, allowing for the identification of bottlenecks and optimization opportunities. The core mechanism focuses on establishing a dynamic complexity landscape, enabling efficient algorithm refinement through automated parameter adjustments. This research aims to provide a more robust and automated approach to algorithm design, ultimately facilitating the creation of more powerful and versatile quantum computations.

title: Quantum State Collapse and Quantum Simulation
abstract: Quantum state collapse is a fundamental process in quantum mechanics, leading to the probabilistic emergence of a single, definite state. This paper explores the potential of leveraging this collapse process within a quantum simulation framework, focusing on the design of an algorithm that utilizes quantum state collapse to accurately model complex quantum systems. We propose a novel approach to simulation that directly incorporates quantum state collapse as a key operational mechanism, aiming to surpass the limitations of traditional methods in simulating intricate quantum systems. The paper details the core mechanism, outlines the simulation algorithm's design, and highlights the significant advantages offered by this integrated approach. We argue that this combined methodology holds the key to unlocking more precise and efficient simulations of complex quantum phenomena.

title: 基于多模态神经元模拟的通用计算架构
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to general computation by leveraging the principles of multimodal neural computation. Traditional artificial neural networks (ANNs) are often limited by their reliance on a single modality of information, hindering their ability to effectively process complex, real-world data. We propose a computational architecture based on simulating multimodal neurons, where synaptic connections model the simultaneous processing of diverse information types – temporal, spatial, and frequency – as is inherent in biological neural systems. The core of our approach involves designing a neural network simulator that accurately mimics the dynamic behavior of these multimodal neurons. This simulator is then integrated into a dedicated computational architecture, enabling the execution of arbitrary computations using the inherent properties of multimodal neural processing. Our system overcomes the modality limitations of conventional ANNs, potentially leading to more efficient and universally applicable computational solutions. The architecture relies on the concept of encoding information across multiple modalities within the neuron's synaptic connections, allowing for parallel and integrated computation. We demonstrate the theoretical feasibility and potential of this architecture, outlining the key components and their interactions.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Encoder (QEIC)
abstract: This paper introduces the Quantum Entanglement Information Encoder (QEIC), a novel approach to information processing leveraging the fundamental principles of quantum entanglement. The core claim of QEIC is to utilize entanglement as the primary mechanism for information encoding and transmission, achieving processing speeds and security levels far exceeding those attainable by classical physics. The proposed system employs an entangled multi-particle system, meticulously controlling the entanglement relationships between particles to achieve efficient information encoding, transmission, and manipulation. Furthermore, the inherent properties of entanglement are exploited for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and quantum computation. We present a theoretical framework for QEIC, outlining the key components and their interactions, and discussing the potential advantages and challenges associated with this technology. The design focuses on maximizing entanglement fidelity and minimizing decoherence effects, critical factors for practical implementation. We explore various encoding schemes based on Bell states and GHZ states, highlighting their unique capabilities for information processing. The QEIC architecture represents a significant departure from conventional information encoding methods, offering a pathway towards fundamentally faster and more secure information technologies.

title: Dynamic Programming for Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Sparse Rewards
abstract: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) offers a promising approach to tackling complex, sparse-reward environments by decomposing problems into smaller, more manageable subtasks. However, traditional dynamic programming (DP) methods often struggle with HRL due to the exponential growth of the state space when multiple levels of abstraction are introduced. This paper presents a novel dynamic programming algorithm designed specifically for HRL with sparse rewards. The core of the algorithm lies in a "level-of-detail" representation, which dynamically adjusts the granularity of the state space at each level of the hierarchy. This adaptation minimizes the state space complexity, enabling efficient learning and improved performance in environments where rewards are infrequent and delayed. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and discuss its potential for real-world applications. The algorithm's key contribution is a practical and scalable method for applying DP to HRL problems, addressing a significant limitation of existing approaches.

title: Adaptive Meta-Learning for Automated Theorem Proving
abstract: Automated theorem proving (ATP) systems have achieved considerable success in specific domains, yet their performance remains significantly hampered by their reliance on hand-crafted heuristics and fixed strategies. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging meta-learning to address this limitation. The core idea is that a meta-learning system can learn to dynamically adapt the proof process itself, optimizing search strategies, heuristics, and proof techniques based on the characteristics of the input theorem. This adaptive approach moves beyond static heuristics, enabling the system to actively learn *how* to learn and prove theorems, resulting in improved performance and robustness. We introduce a framework where the meta-learner observes the theorem proving process and adjusts its parameters to maximize proof success. The presented system demonstrates the potential of meta-learning to significantly enhance the capabilities of ATP systems.

title: Differential Privacy via Randomized Graph Traversal
abstract: This paper introduces a novel differential privacy (DP) mechanism leveraging randomized graph traversal. Existing DP techniques frequently suffer from substantial performance penalties and accuracy degradation. Our approach addresses these limitations by incorporating the inherent structure of graphs into the privacy-preserving process. Specifically, we randomly sample paths through the graph during computations, enabling the algorithm to achieve DP guarantees while minimizing the detrimental impact on accuracy. title: Adaptive Evolution Based on Biological Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to program adaptation and evolution by leveraging the mechanisms of synaptic plasticity found within biological neural networks. The core concept involves constructing a computational model mimicking a biological neural network, enabling programs to autonomously adapt and evolve within complex environments through simulated synaptic plasticity. Specifically, the program adjusts its code structure and parameters based on environmental feedback, mirroring the learning process observed in biological systems. Unlike traditional methods such as genetic algorithms, this approach directly utilizes the inherent adaptability of neural networks, offering a potentially more efficient and robust path to program evolution. The research investigates the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach, demonstrating the potential for self-optimization and adaptation without explicit human intervention. The presented methodology provides a framework for future research into biologically inspired adaptive systems.

title: Explainable AI for Hardware Design using Neural-Symbolic Interfaces
abstract: The increasing reliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) for hardware design necessitates a critical examination of its decision-making processes. Deep neural networks, while effective in optimizing hardware architectures, often operate as "black boxes," hindering trust and impeding widespread adoption. This work proposes a novel approach to address this explainability challenge by introducing a neural-symbolic interface. The core idea is to bridge the gap between the complex, distributed representations learned by deep neural networks and human-understandable symbolic explanations derived from established hardware design rules. This interface translates the output of the neural network (denoted as *SNN*) into a structured, interpretable representation (*SSY*) based on logical rules and constraints. We define this relationship as: *SSY* = *f(SNN, R)*, where *R* represents a set of hardware design rules. This allows users to understand the rationale behind the AI's design choices, fostering confidence and enabling informed decision-making. The system is designed to provide a level of transparency into the AI's reasoning, ultimately facilitating the integration of AI into hardware design workflows. This approach moves beyond simple feature attribution and provides a truly explainable representation of the AI's internal processes.

title: Fusing Spectral Signatures and Activation Clustering for Backdoor Detection in Healthcare Imaging Models: Method, Implementation, and Evaluation
abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly deployed in healthcare imaging pipelines for diagnosticsupport, yet the security of these models against training-time attacks — particularlydata poisoning and backdoor insertion — remains substantially under-tested relative to theirgrowing deployment. Recent healthcare-sector guidance (Health Sector Coordinating CouncilCybersecurity Working Group, 2025) and federal policy (Executive Order 14409, 2026) have explicitlynamed data poisoning and model manipulation as threats requiring dedicated defenses,yet no widely adopted, openly available detection tooling validated specifically on healthcareimaging benchmarks currently exists. This paper proposes a detection methodology combiningspectral signature analysis (Tran et al., 2018) and activation clustering (Chen et al., 2018) —two established backdoor-detection techniques not yet systematically benchmarked together onpublic healthcare imaging datasets — and specifies an evaluation protocol against syntheticallypoisoned variants of public medical imaging benchmarks alongside a non-healthcare criticalinfrastructure-relevant dataset, to test cross-sector generalizability. We frame the resultingevidence output against the NIST AI Risk Management Framework’s Measure function and theMITRE ATLAS adversary technique taxonomy, so that results are directly usable by healthcaresecurity teams rather than requiring translation from research notation. This paper presents themethodology and evaluation plan; empirical results will be reported in a follow-up publication.

title: Decomposing LLM-Judge Uncertainty to Target Expert Labels
abstract: An LLM judge evaluates outputs at scale. Experts should label only where it is least sure. Its natural escalation signal conflates two uncertainties: aleatoric, real disagreement in the expert pool, which labels cannot reduce, and epistemic, the judge's ignorance, which labels do reduce. A small Bayesian model separates them: a regression on labels already collected learns how far to trust a black-box judge's prediction. Both components follow as simple formulas, with no sampling or further judge calls. The components isolate on a real LLM judge against exactly known truth, and stated confidence is no guide to its actual error. On real human disagreement (ChaosNLI) the epistemic ranking removes 83% more error than total uncertainty for the same expert labels, though simply escalating the least-labelled items does as well there. We demonstrate we can estimate where a judge is ignorant rather than where experts genuinely disagree, and propose using this to direct expert labelling. Code and data are available at https://github.com/composo-ai/judge-uncertainty-decomposition.

title: A Multi-Layer Security Framework for Prompt Injection and Knowledge Poisoning Mitigation in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factual usefulness of Large Language Models (LLMs) by grounding generation in external knowledge. When RAG is combined with autonomous agents, the system can plan multi-step tasks, retrieve information, and invoke external tools, but the additional autonomy also creates new attack surfaces. This paper proposes a Multi-Layer Security Framework (MLSF) for agentic RAG systems that combines input inspection, retrieved-context security, provenance verification, tool authorization, and output verification. The framework is designed around a practical Python technology stack consisting of LangChain, LangGraph, Mistral Small, embeddings, ChromaDB, FastAPI, and Docker. A controlled evaluation environment is defined with five attack categories: direct prompt injection, indirect prompt injection, knowledge poisoning, tool misuse, and context manipulation.

title: Title: Algorithmic Complexity of Cognitive Models
abstract: Cognitive models, representing the internal workings of the human mind, are fundamentally complex systems. Quantifying this complexity is a significant challenge, and existing methods often rely on approximations and subjective interpretations. This paper explores a novel approach to rigorously quantify the algorithmic complexity of cognitive models, leveraging the concept of "cognitive space" and its connection to computational complexity. We propose a new metric, termed the "Cognitive Space Density" (CSD), designed to capture the inherent difficulty of simulating or reasoning about a cognitive system within a defined space. The core mechanism revolves around establishing a quantifiable measure of the space's dimensionality and the relationships between elements within it, ultimately providing a pathway towards a more precise understanding of cognitive limitations and the potential for algorithmic optimization. This work aims to move beyond simplistic approximations and offer a potentially transformative methodology for analyzing and modeling cognitive processes.

title: Title: Information-Theoretic Constraint Optimization for Adaptive Data Structures
abstract: This paper explores the application of information theory, specifically entropy and mutual information, to enhance the design and evolution of adaptive data structures. Traditional data structure optimization often relies on static cost functions, neglecting the inherent information content of the data. We propose a novel constraint optimization algorithm that actively seeks to maximize information, thereby driving the data structure to dynamically adapt to changing demands. This approach leverages entropy and mutual information to create structures that are robust and efficiently utilize available resources. The core mechanism focuses on quantifying and exploiting the information density within the data, forcing the structure to evolve in a manner that maximizes this information metric. This research presents a framework for real-time adaptation, offering a potential shift from brittle static optimization to a more responsive and intelligent data structure management system.

title: Adaptive Chaos Theory & Dynamic Constraint Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the integration of adaptive chaos theory and dynamic constraint optimization to address complex optimization problems. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with dynamic and evolving constraints, leading to suboptimal solutions. We propose a novel algorithmic framework centered around a feedback loop that continuously monitors system performance against constraints using a chaos-theoretic model. This model predicts future constraint shifts, triggering reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust the constraints for stability and efficiency. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop, a reinforcement learning component, and a chaotic model to achieve adaptive and resilient solutions. This work presents a new approach to optimization that surpasses existing methods in its ability to handle dynamically changing constraints.

title: 基于自适应的神经网络的隐式特征选择算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for implicit feature selection using a dynamically adjusted neural network. Traditional feature selection techniques often rely on fixed feature weights, limiting the model's ability to effectively capture complex relationships within the data. This work explores a new approach that dynamically adjusts the weights of the neural network to enhance the model's generalization performance. The core mechanism involves a self-supervised learning framework where the network learns a representation of the data and subsequently adjusts the feature weights to optimize for predictive accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through experiments on a variety of datasets, revealing significant improvements in model performance compared to existing techniques. This innovation offers a more flexible and adaptive approach to feature selection, potentially leading to more robust and accurate models.

title: Bayesian Fractal Geometry (BFG)
abstract: This paper introduces Bayesian Fractal Geometry (BFG), a novel framework for representing and modeling complex probability distributions through a combination of Bayesian inference and fractal geometry. The core idea is to formalize the concept of "fractalized Bayesian inference," allowing for highly accurate modeling of non-stationary environments. We propose a probabilistic framework that dynamically updates the probability distribution based on observation, utilizing fractal geometry to represent uncertainty. This approach offers significant advantages over traditional methods, particularly in scenarios where environments exhibit complex, non-linear changes over time. The development of BFG aims to revolutionize fields reliant on probabilistic modeling, offering a more robust and adaptable representation of uncertainty.

title: Self-Organizing Map (SOM) Deep Learning Acceleration Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel deep learning acceleration algorithm based on Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs). We propose an optimized parameterization strategy for SOMs to enhance their learning and prediction capabilities, particularly when dealing with complex topological structures. The core mechanism centers around leveraging the inherent self-organizing properties of SOMs to reduce computational demands and accelerate learning, offering a significant improvement over existing methods. This algorithm focuses on optimizing the network's structure through a refined parameterization process, ultimately leading to faster and more efficient deep learning models. We present preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in a variety of datasets, showcasing its potential to accelerate deep learning tasks.
